bib.title: Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; some summarization table rows skimmed.

question: Does training a language model to predict the next n tokens at once with n output heads on a shared trunk improve downstream quality and inference speed over next-token prediction?
hypothesis: Multi-token prediction as an auxiliary loss improves sample efficiency and generative abilities (especially code) at larger scale, by reducing the teacher-forcing/autoregressive mismatch.
contributions: A simple multi-token prediction architecture with no train time or memory overhead (Section 2).
Experimental evidence that it is beneficial at scale, with models up to 13B parameters solving around 15% more code problems on average (Section 3).
Multi-token prediction enables self-speculative decoding, making models up to 3 times faster at inference time across a wide range of batch-sizes (Section 3.2).

method.summary: A shared transformer trunk feeds n independent transformer-layer heads with a shared unembedding; loss is the sum of n cross-entropies for tokens t+1..t+n. Heads are added by removing n-1 trunk layers to keep parameters equal. Heads are run forward/backward sequentially to save memory; inference uses the next-token head or self-speculative decoding.
method.task: next-token vs multi-token pretraining of decoder-only LMs on code and natural language; evaluated on code generation, summarization, GSM8K, synthetic tasks

datasets.name: Code corpus (unnamed)
datasets.preprocessing: 32k-token tokenizer; byte-level variant uses replicated unembeddings

datasets.name: CodeContests
datasets.split: Python subset, train split with correct/incorrect annotations; test split for eval

datasets.name: 8 summarization sets (CNN/DailyMail, Multi-News, OrangeSum, pn-summary, SAMSum, ThaiSum, WikiSummary, XSum) plus BigPatent in Table S13
Children stories; books mix 9:1
datasets.preprocessing: character names replaced with random two-token names

models.name: Multi-token predictor (n=2,4,6,8; byte-level n=8, 16, 32)
models.architecture: shared transformer trunk + n transformer-layer heads + shared unembedding

training.objective: L_n = -sum_t sum_{i=1..n} log P(x_{t+i} | z_{t:1}), n heads; parameter-matched by removing n-1 trunk layers
training.optimizer: Adam, beta1 0.9, beta2 0.95, decoupled weight decay 0.1
training.lr_schedule: linear warmup then cosine decay to fraction of peak (decay ratio 0.03; 0.10 for language models; 0.004 CodeContests)
training.batch_size: 8 x 2^20 tokens (7 x 2^20 for 500B/1T code; 12 x 2^20 bytes; 0.25 x 2^20 synthetic)
training.seeds: two runs per config for synthetic tasks; otherwise not stated

other.batch_size_unit: Table S13 header says Batch size (2^20); inferred to be tokens

inference.decoding: Pass@k sampling for code; greedy self-speculative decoding for speed
inference.temperature: oracle temperature per model/dataset/pass@k (Table S12); 0.5-0.9 CodeContests; 0.2-1.4 GSM8K
inference.samples: 200 samples per problem (Table 1); 1000 (Fig 3, Fig 4); 200 for GSM8K

metrics.name: pass@k (k=1,10,100)
metrics.definition: unbiased estimator of Chen et al. 2021

metrics.name: ROUGE-L F1
metrics.definition: LCS overlap F1, best validation checkpoint

metrics.name: relative speedup
metrics.definition: decoding speed relative to autoregressive k=1 at same batch size

eval.protocol: Bootstrapped 90% CIs in Fig 1 and 3; oracle temperature chosen on test scores; epoch oracle for induction.

evidence.quote: The temperatures were chosen optimally (based on test scores; i.e. these are oracle temperatures)

results.quote: Our 13B parameter models solves 12 % more problems on HumanEval and 17 % more on MBPP than comparable next-token models.

results.setup: 13B, 209.7B code tokens, Table S7

results.claim: Multi-token prediction is worse than baseline at small sizes and better at scale.
results.setup: Six sizes 0.3B-13B trained on 91B (<=3B) or 209.7B (7B, 13B) code tokens, MBPP/HumanEval pass@1,10,100 with 1000 samples
results.quote: Multi-token prediction models are worse than the baseline for small model sizes, but outperform the baseline at scale.

results.setup: 7B 4-token model, 1T code tokens, 4200 sequences of 512 tokens, 512-token greedy completions, batch size 42; 3.50 tokens/forward
results.table: Table S2, row 4 heads, column Code Rel. speedup

results.claim: Multi-byte prediction (n=8) beats next-byte prediction on MBPP and HumanEval pass@1.
results.setup: 7B byte-level, 313B bytes of code (0.5 epoch), 200 samples per problem, oracle temperature
results.quote: solving 67% more problems on MBPP pass@1 and 20% more problems on HumanEval pass@1.

results.claim: 4-token prediction best n on 7B/200B-token code: MBPP gains +3.8%, +2.1%, +3.2% at pass@1,10,100.
results.setup: 7B, 200B code tokens, n in {1,2,4,6,8}, 32k vocab, oracle temperature, 200 samples per problem
results.quote: +3.8%, +2.1% and +3.2% for MBPP and +1.2%, +3.7% and +4.1% for HumanEval.
results.note: Gains are absolute points vs n=1; Table 1 n=4 MBPP 33.8/55.9/76.9 vs 30.0/53.8/73.7.

results.claim: On APPS/Intro n=6 is best, so optimal n depends on data.
results.setup: 7B, 200B code tokens
results.quote: Interestingly, for APPS/Intro, n = 6 takes the lead with +0.7%, +3.0% and +5.3%.

results.setup: 7B, 1T code tokens (4 epochs), n=4 vs n=1, oracle temperature

results.claim: Fine-tuning on CodeContests: both 4-token-pretrained variants beat next-token baseline on pass@k across k.
results.setup: 7B models, CodeContests Python train split, 1000 samples per test problem, T in {0.5..0.9}, max over T
results.quote: both ways of finetuning the 4-token prediction model outperform the next-token prediction baseline.

results.claim: On 6 standard multiple-choice/likelihood NLP benchmarks, n=2 matches baseline and n=4 regresses.
results.setup: 7B, 200B natural-language tokens
results.quote: The 2 future token model has the same performance as the baseline and the 4 future token model regresses a bit.

results.claim: Average summarization ROUGE-L F1 improves with n=2 and n=4, gap shrinking with more data.
results.setup: 7B, 200B tokens, n=2 (26.23+0.51), 8 summarization datasets, finetuned 3 epochs, best-val checkpoint
results.table: Table S9, row Average, columns Baseline 200B and Delta n=2
results.note: Value is the printed delta of n=2 over baseline 26.23. At 500B: baseline 27.08, +0.28 (n=2), +0.31 (n=4); 200B n=4 +0.46.

results.claim: GSM8K 8-shot: n=2 better at 200B tokens, order reverses at 500B; n=4 worse throughout.
results.setup: 7B, 200B and 500B language tokens, 8-shot, nucleus p=0.95, temps 0.2-1.4
results.quote: For 200B training tokens, the n = 2 model clearly outperforms the next-token prediction baseline, while the pattern reverses after 500B tokens and n = 4 is worse throughout.

results.claim: 2-token loss greatly improves induction formation for small models; advantage vanishes at ~100M non-embedding params.
results.setup: 1M-1B non-embedding params, children stories, up to 90 epochs with epoch oracle, two seeds, 100 test stories with random two-token names
results.quote: We find that 2-token prediction loss leads to a vastly improved formation of induction capability for models of size 30M nonembedding parameters and below, with their advantage disappearing for sizes of 100M nonembedding parameters and above.

results.claim: Multi-token prediction improves polynomial-arithmetic accuracy, including out-of-domain, more than tripling model size.
results.setup: 30M and 100M models, F7[X]/(X^5), greedy, 2000 test samples per operation count, two runs per config
results.quote: Tripling the model size, on the other hand, has a considerably smaller effect than replacing next-token prediction with multi-token prediction loss (Figure S16).

results.claim: Training time overhead of n=4 relative to n=1 is 7-22%, n=2 2-7%.
results.setup: FSDP implementation; 0.3B n=4 is 1.22, 13B n=4 1.09
results.note: Abstract says no overhead in training time; Table S5 shows a slight overhead the authors attribute to suboptimal FSDP use.

results.claim: Peak GPU memory reduced from O(nV+d) to O(V+d) via sequential head forward/backward.
results.setup: Section 2 implementation claim, no measurement
results.quote: we have reduced the peak GPU memory utilization from O(nV + d) to O(V + d), at no expense in runtime (Table S5).

limits: Oracle temperatures chosen on test scores in Table 1 and Fig 4, which can favour all models but is a tuned test-set protocol.
Multi-token prediction is worse than baseline for small models and hurts on multiple-choice NLP at 7B (n=4).
Optimal n depends on data (n=4 for MBPP/HumanEval, n=6 for APPS/Intro) and is not chosen automatically.
GSM8K advantage for n=2 reverses at 500B tokens, n=4 worse throughout.
Fine-tuning Llama 2 with the loss gave no significant gain.
Explanations in Sec 5 are speculation; computation-sharing hypothesis not confirmed (App K).
Training data sources, seeds, precision and code release are not stated in text; experiments up to 7B/1T tokens (13B only 209.7B tokens).
Abstract claims no training-time overhead but Table S5 shows 2-22% overhead.
